meta.title: Human Rights
meta.range: HSC core · Part II · 20% of course time

boxes.label: Mandatory core
boxes.bodyHtml: Human Rights is compulsory for every HSC Legal Studies student and is tested in every real exam — Section I (multiple choice, shared with Crime) and Section II Part A (short answer, worth 15 marks across three questions) of the HSC paper draw directly on this topic.

boxes.label: Aligned to the HSC syllabus
boxes.bodyHtml: Quiz, trivia and practice content here is written to the NESA Legal Studies Stage 6 Syllabus and modelled on real HSC exam question styles and marking criteria.

summary.note: Covers all three syllabus sub-topics of the Human Rights core, in NESA's own order.

groups.title: The nature and development of human rights
points: Human rights are the basic rights and freedoms belonging to every person, simply because they are human, regardless of nationality, sex, ethnicity or any other status.

Human rights have developed and expanded over time in response to changing values, including the abolition of slavery, trade unionism and labour rights, universal suffrage (the right to vote regardless of gender, race or status), universal education, self-determination, environmental rights and peace rights.

Universal suffrage developed gradually: the UK's Representation of the People Act 1918 first extended the vote to a majority of men and some women; the movement gained global recognition afterwards, including the 19th Amendment to the US Constitution (1920) and Australia's Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902, which enfranchised most women — though First Nations peoples in Australia did not gain full, unrestricted access to enrol and vote in federal elections until 1962.

Formal statements of human rights include the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) (1948) — a declaration, not a binding treaty, that sets out fundamental rights including the right to vote (Article 21) — the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) (1966) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) (1966), which together with the UDHR are often called the 'International Bill of Rights'.

groups.title: Promoting and enforcing human rights
points: In the international community, state sovereignty means a state generally cannot be forced to comply with a human rights instrument it hasn't agreed to — signing a treaty shows intent to be bound, but a treaty is only legally binding on a state once it has been ratified (formally consented to) by that state.

The United Nations promotes human rights partly through bodies like the Human Rights Committee, which monitors state compliance with treaties like the ICCPR that they've ratified. Intergovernmental organisations (made up of member states, e.g. the United Nations itself) differ from courts/tribunals (e.g. the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals for the most serious international crimes) and from non-government organisations and the media, which promote human rights without formal legal enforcement power.

In Australia, human rights are incorporated into domestic law through the Constitution (including the division of powers between the Commonwealth and the states, and the separation of powers between Parliament, the executive and the courts), statute law and common law, rather than through one single, comprehensive Charter of Rights.

The division of powers has been used to protect human rights: in Commonwealth v Tasmania (1983) (the Tasmanian Dam Case), the High Court used the Commonwealth's external affairs power to stop a dam and protect a World Heritage site; in Commonwealth v Australian Capital Territory (2013), the High Court struck down the ACT's same-sex marriage law as inconsistent with Commonwealth marriage legislation, showing the division of powers can work in different directions depending on the case.

Arguments for an Australian Charter of Rights include that it would raise public awareness of rights and provide clearer legal protection than relying on scattered statutes and common law; arguments against include that it could transfer too much power to unelected judges over democratically elected parliament, and that existing protections (constitutional, statutory and common law) are already considered adequate by critics of a Charter.

Statutory bodies such as the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) investigate complaints of discrimination and can attempt conciliation between parties, while courts and tribunals can hear and enforce breaches of specific statutes such as anti-discrimination law — but neither can override valid Commonwealth legislation, since Australia has no single overriding Charter of Rights.

Non-government organisations (e.g. Amnesty International, the Red Cross) and the media play an important role domestically and internationally by investigating and publicising human rights abuses, applying public and political pressure for reform, even though they lack any formal power to enforce compliance themselves.

groups.title: Promoting and enforcing human rights — a contemporary issue
points: Contemporary human rights issues that illustrate both the promotion and the limits of enforcement include genocide, the treatment of refugees and asylum seekers, child soldiers, torture, capital punishment, arbitrary detention, discrimination (religious, gender-based or otherwise), exploitation of workers, and human trafficking and modern slavery.

Human trafficking and slavery: in R v Tang (2008), the High Court clarified the legal meaning of 'slavery' under Australian law, strengthening later prosecutions. Parliament has since reformed the law further — the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Slavery, Slavery-like Conditions and People Trafficking) Act 2013 (Cth) added specific offences (forced marriage, forced labour, organ trafficking) to the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth), and the Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth) requires large businesses operating in Australia to report annually on modern slavery risks in their supply chains — though under-reporting means not all victims are identified or assisted.

Ad hoc tribunals have enforced human rights after mass atrocities with mixed success. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), established in 1994/1995, sentenced 62 people and acquitted 14, was the first tribunal to recognise rape as an instrument of genocide and the first to interpret the definition of genocide from the 1948 Genocide Convention, but it never indicted a single member of the Rwandan Patriotic Front, drawing criticism for one-sided 'victor's justice'. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), established in 1993, sentenced 90 and acquitted 19, including senior leaders like Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić (both given life sentences), and gave around 4,650 witnesses a voice — but Slobodan Milošević died before his trial concluded, and controversial partial acquittals and plea deals were criticised as too lenient.

The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (established 2003), set up to prosecute the Khmer Rouge genocide (an estimated 1.3 to 2 million deaths), has to date convicted only a small handful of individuals despite operating for over a decade at a cost of hundreds of millions of US dollars — illustrating that ad hoc tribunals, while historically important for establishing precedent, can be slow, expensive and limited in how many perpetrators they actually bring to justice.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how the division of powers can protect human rights in Australia. Use an appropriate example to support your answer.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain what the division of powers is.
  • Show how it can be used to protect human rights.
  • Integrate one specific example (a real High Court case).
Sample answer

The division of powers separates law-making responsibility between the Commonwealth and state parliaments under the Constitution. This can protect human rights because it allows the Commonwealth to legislate in areas — like external affairs — that a state government might not, or might act against.

In Commonwealth v Tasmania (1983) (the Tasmanian Dam Case), the High Court found the Commonwealth's external affairs power under s51(xxix) of the Constitution allowed it to stop the Tasmanian government from constructing a dam that would have destroyed a World Heritage-listed area, because Australia had international obligations under the World Heritage Convention. This shows the division of powers can protect rights (including environmental and cultural heritage protections) even when a state government's own priorities conflict with them — although the division of powers can also work the other way, as shown when the High Court struck down the ACT's same-sex marriage law in 2013 for being inconsistent with Commonwealth marriage legislation, illustrating that the division of powers protects rights only when the Commonwealth chooses to exercise its power in a rights-protective direction.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the role of law reform in protecting human rights. Support your response with reference to ONE contemporary human rights issue.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define law reform.
  • Explain how it protects human rights generally.
  • Integrate one contemporary issue with real legislation/cases.
Sample answer

Law reform refers to changes in the law, made by Parliament or the courts, in response to society's evolving understanding of justice. Law reform can protect human rights by strengthening existing legal protections or by creating entirely new ones as new issues are recognised.

Human trafficking and slavery illustrate this well. In R v Tang (2008), the High Court clarified the legal meaning of "slavery" under Australian law, strengthening the basis for future prosecutions. Parliament then went further: the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Slavery, Slavery-like Conditions and People Trafficking) Act 2013 (Cth) amended the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) to add specific offences — including forced marriage, forced labour and organ trafficking — better reflecting international instruments like the UN's Trafficking Protocol. The Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth) went further still, requiring large businesses operating in Australia to report annually on the risk of slavery in their supply chains. However, law reform has limits: under-reporting of trafficking and slavery means many victims are never identified, regardless of how strong the legal framework becomes — showing that law reform can strengthen protection for human rights, but cannot guarantee it is enforced in every case.

questions.questionHtml: Using examples, evaluate the extent to which ad hoc tribunals have been effective in enforcing human rights.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain what an ad hoc tribunal is.
  • Discuss at least two tribunals, with real statistics/examples.
  • Weigh strengths and limitations to reach a judgement.
Sample answer

Ad hoc tribunals are courts created under UN authority to address specific human rights abuses, and have been effective in enforcing human rights to a considerable, though not complete, extent. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), created in 1994/1995, successfully prosecuted 62 of 76 individuals it tried in relation to the 1994 genocide of the Tutsi minority, and was the first tribunal to recognise rape as an instrument of genocide and to interpret the definition of genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention, entrenching important legal precedent for future prosecutions. Similarly, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), created in 1993, sentenced 90 individuals — including senior leadership such as Radovan Karadžić — and gave roughly 4,650 witnesses of the Yugoslav Wars a chance to be heard.

However, both tribunals had real limitations: the ICTR never indicted a single member of the Rwandan Patriotic Front despite allegations against them, creating a perception of one-sided "victor's justice", while the ICTY's partial acquittal of Vojislav Šešelj and lenient plea deal for Biljana Plavšić were both criticised, and Slobodan Milošević died before his trial could conclude. The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia illustrate the limits even more starkly: despite over $300 million USD in costs and eleven years of operation, only a handful of individuals have been convicted in relation to a genocide that killed over a million people. Overall, ad hoc tribunals have been effective to a moderate extent — they establish important legal precedent and give victims a voice, but their narrow scope, cost and slow pace mean most perpetrators of mass atrocities are never actually brought before them.

questions.questionHtml: Explain the role of the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) in promoting human rights domestically.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain what the AHRC does.
  • Note its limitation.
Sample answer

The Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) investigates complaints of discrimination and human rights breaches under Commonwealth anti-discrimination law, and can attempt conciliation between the parties to resolve a complaint without the need for court proceedings. It also has an educative role, publishing reports and conducting inquiries into specific human rights issues to raise public awareness.

However, the AHRC cannot make binding orders or override valid Commonwealth legislation — if conciliation fails, a complainant must pursue their matter through the Federal Court, and the Commission's own recommendations are not legally enforceable. This means the AHRC is an important promotional and conciliatory body, but not itself a source of binding legal enforcement.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the effectiveness of non-government organisations in promoting human rights.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Give examples of NGOs and what they do.
  • Weigh strengths against the key limitation.
  • Reach a judgement.
Sample answer

Non-government organisations such as Amnesty International and the Red Cross investigate and publicise human rights abuses, applying public and diplomatic pressure on governments to reform — the Red Cross also plays a direct, practical role under the Geneva Conventions, monitoring the treatment of prisoners of war and civilians during armed conflict.

NGOs can be highly effective at raising international awareness of abuses, including in situations where the offending government itself is unwilling to acknowledge the problem. However, they have no formal legal power to compel a state to change its laws or conduct, and their effectiveness depends heavily on being able to access affected regions and populations — access that authoritarian states can, and do, restrict. Overall, NGOs are an important complement to legal enforcement mechanisms, but cannot substitute for binding legal action when a state is determined to resist reform.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how the separation of powers can help protect human rights in Australia.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define the separation of powers.
  • Explain how it protects rights.
  • Note a limitation.
Sample answer

The separation of powers divides law-making (Parliament), law-execution (the executive) and law-interpretation (the courts) between different bodies, so that no single arm of government holds all governmental power.

This helps protect human rights because an independent judiciary can review executive action and, in some cases, find legislation invalid — for example, if it is inconsistent with the Constitution — providing a check on the other two arms of government that could otherwise infringe on individual rights without any independent oversight. However, Australia's separation of powers mainly restrains federal judicial power rather than guaranteeing specific rights directly, so it protects rights indirectly, by checking how power is exercised, rather than by setting out a comprehensive list of protected rights the way a Charter of Rights would.

groups.title: The nature and development of human rights

questions.questionHtml: Assess the role of state sovereignty in promoting and enforcing human rights.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define state sovereignty.
  • Give an example of it helping and an example of it hindering human rights.
  • Reach a judgement.
Sample answer

State sovereignty — the right of a nation-state to govern itself and make decisions within its own jurisdiction without outside interference — acts as both a support and a barrier to protecting human rights. It can support human rights when a state chooses to adopt international instruments into domestic law: Australia's ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, given effect through the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth), is one example of sovereignty being used to strengthen rights protection domestically.

However, sovereignty can also limit the protection of human rights, since a state cannot generally be forced to comply with an instrument it hasn't ratified, or to allow outside intervention even during serious abuses. This is illustrated by the international community's slow response to events like the Rwandan genocide, where the principle of non-interference in a sovereign state's internal affairs contributed to delayed international action. The United Nations Security Council, in particular, can be limited by sovereignty concerns and the veto power held by its five permanent members, which can prevent binding action even where mass human rights violations are occurring. Overall, state sovereignty is a double-edged principle: essential to the stability of international relations, but capable of being used by states to resist scrutiny of their own human rights record.

questions.questionHtml: Discuss the arguments for and against an Australian Charter of Rights.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain what a Charter of Rights is.
  • Give at least one argument for and one against.
  • Note Australia's current alternative protections.
Sample answer

Unlike many other countries, Australia has no single, comprehensive Charter of Rights — human rights are instead protected through a mix of the Constitution, ordinary statutes, and common law. Arguments for introducing a Charter include that it would raise public awareness and understanding of rights, and provide clearer, more consistent legal protection than relying on rights being scattered across different laws that can be amended or repealed by an ordinary parliamentary majority.

Arguments against a Charter include the concern that it would transfer significant power from democratically elected parliaments to unelected judges, who would be responsible for interpreting and applying broadly worded rights in individual cases. Critics also argue existing protections — including the division and separation of powers, specific anti-discrimination statutes, and common law protections built up through case law — already provide adequate protection without the risk of over-judicialising political questions. Ultimately, the debate reflects a broader tension between the certainty a codified Charter could offer and the flexibility of Australia's current, more piecemeal approach to protecting human rights.

questions.questionHtml: Outline the significance of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) 1948.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • State when and why it was adopted.
  • Explain its legal status.
  • Explain its lasting significance.
Sample answer

The UDHR was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948, in the aftermath of the Second World War, as the first comprehensive international statement of fundamental human rights covering civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights. It is a declaration, not a binding treaty, so it does not itself create enforceable legal obligations.

Its significance lies in what it made possible afterwards: it provided the foundation for later binding treaties, including the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966), and remains hugely influential today, having shaped human rights protections and constitutions in many countries since.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how universal suffrage developed as a human right over time.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Give at least two real milestones, in order.
  • Show the development was gradual and uneven, not immediate.
Sample answer

Universal suffrage — the right to vote regardless of gender, race or status — developed gradually rather than all at once. The UK's Representation of the People Act 1918 first extended the vote to a majority of men and some women, and similar expansions followed soon after in other countries, including the 19th Amendment to the US Constitution (1920) and Australia's Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902, which enfranchised most women.

However, this expansion was uneven: First Nations peoples in Australia did not gain full, unrestricted access to enrol and vote in federal elections until 1962 — over sixty years after the Commonwealth Franchise Act. This shows universal suffrage developing as a human right through a long series of separate, incremental legal changes in response to shifting social values, rather than through a single moment of recognition.

questions.questionHtml: Assess the significance of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) to the development of international human rights law.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain what each covenant covers.
  • Explain why they were significant compared to the UDHR alone.
  • Note a limitation.
Sample answer

The ICCPR and ICESCR, both adopted in 1966, split the broad aspirations of the 1948 UDHR into two separate binding treaties — the ICCPR covering civil and political rights (such as the right to a fair trial and freedom of expression), and the ICESCR covering economic, social and cultural rights (such as the right to work, education and health).

Their significance lies in making parts of the UDHR's aspirations legally binding for the first time on states that ratify them, rather than remaining purely declaratory — the Human Rights Committee, for example, monitors state compliance with the ICCPR. However, like any treaty, both covenants are only binding on states that ratify them, and enforcement still depends heavily on state cooperation, since there is no external body able to force a non-compliant state to change its domestic law or practice.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)?
trivia.answerHtml: A 1948 UN declaration (not a binding treaty) setting out fundamental human rights, including the right to vote.

trivia.questionHtml: What two covenants, together with the UDHR, form the 'International Bill of Rights'?
trivia.answerHtml: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), both 1966.

trivia.questionHtml: What does it mean for a state to 'ratify' a treaty?
trivia.answerHtml: To formally consent to be legally bound by it — signing alone shows intent, but ratification (and often domestic legislation) is needed to make it binding.

trivia.questionHtml: What body monitors state compliance with the ICCPR?
What is the difference between an intergovernmental organisation and a non-government organisation?
trivia.answerHtml: An intergovernmental organisation (e.g. the United Nations) is made up of member states; an NGO is independent of government and promotes human rights without formal legal enforcement power.

trivia.questionHtml: What did Commonwealth v Tasmania (1983) (the Tasmanian Dam Case) establish?
trivia.answerHtml: That the Commonwealth's external affairs power can be used to fulfil Australia's international obligations, even against a state government's wishes.

trivia.questionHtml: What happened in Commonwealth v Australian Capital Territory (2013)?
trivia.answerHtml: The High Court struck down the ACT's same-sex marriage law as inconsistent with Commonwealth marriage legislation.

trivia.questionHtml: Name one argument for an Australian Charter of Rights.
trivia.answerHtml: It would raise public awareness and provide clearer, more consistent legal protection of rights.

trivia.questionHtml: Name one argument against an Australian Charter of Rights.
trivia.answerHtml: It could transfer significant power from elected parliaments to unelected judges.

trivia.questionHtml: What did R v Tang (2008) clarify?
trivia.answerHtml: The legal meaning of 'slavery' under Australian law, strengthening later trafficking prosecutions.

trivia.questionHtml: What does the Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth) require?
trivia.answerHtml: Large businesses operating in Australia to report annually on the risk of modern slavery in their supply chains.

trivia.questionHtml: When was the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) established, and what genocide did it address?
trivia.answerHtml: 1994/1995, addressing the genocide of the Tutsi minority in Rwanda.

trivia.questionHtml: What was the ICTR the first tribunal to do?
trivia.answerHtml: The first to recognise rape as an instrument of genocide, and the first to interpret the definition of genocide from the 1948 Genocide Convention.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a major criticism of the ICTR?
trivia.answerHtml: It never indicted a single member of the Rwandan Patriotic Front, despite allegations against them.

trivia.questionHtml: When was the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) established?
Name one senior leader sentenced by the ICTY and their sentence.
trivia.answerHtml: Radovan Karadžić (Bosnian Serb political leader) or Ratko Mladić (Bosnian Serb general) — both given life sentences.

trivia.answerHtml: He died before the trial concluded.

trivia.answerHtml: Despite over $300 million USD in costs and 11+ years of operation, only a handful of individuals have been convicted for the Khmer Rouge genocide.

trivia.questionHtml: What role does the International Criminal Court (ICC) play?
trivia.answerHtml: It prosecutes individuals for the most serious international crimes, such as genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

When did First Nations peoples gain unrestricted access to enrol and vote in Australian federal elections?

trivia.answerHtml: The media — raising public awareness of human rights abuses without formal legal enforcement power.
